sourceCaveat: The original book edition has not been independently checked. See the listed source on Sources for attribution limits.

strict.criterion: More than half of learning is supplied by intelligent simulated teachers, rather than human instruction or ordinary learning resources.
strict.rationale: 2019 classroom and distance learning did not predominantly use intelligent simulated teachers. AI tutoring is a growing capability, but teacher-based education and other learning remain central. A video lecture or web page is not automatically an intelligent tutor.

evidence.title: NCES: Teachers’ use of educational technology in 2009
evidence.note: Primary institutional, research, or issuer source. Dates in the claim refer to the observation or product event, not the review date.

evidence.title: NCES: School technology support during COVID
evidence.note: 96% of public schools provided devices to students who needed them by 2021–22; 23% assigned take-home devices to all students before COVID. Not proof every student owned a sub-pound tablet.

evidence.title: UNESCO: Teachers cannot be coded
evidence.note: Institutional context on continuing human teachers, shortages and AI assistance. Normative guidance is not a statistical census of all learning hours.

broader.criterion: AI tutoring and interactive digital software become widely available learning aids alongside human teachers.
broader.rationale: Interactive educational software and generative-AI study assistants are widely used by students in 2026, earning partial credit. Even under a charitable reading, human teachers, classrooms, and traditional study remain central—not displaced by simulated AI tutors delivering most learning.
changedConditions: Credits widespread digital and AI tutoring aids as partial without relaxing away the 'most learning' claim
